mn74:1.2: On one occasion the Blessed One was living at Rājagaha on Vulture Peak Mountain, in the Boar’s Cave.
mn74:2.1: Then Dīghanakha the Wanderer went to the Blessed One and exchanged greetings with him.
mn74:2.2: When the courteous and amiable talk was finished, he stood at one side. Standing at one side, Dīghanakha the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:
mn74:2.3: “Master Gotama, this is my doctrine, this is my view:
mn74:2.6: ‘I have no liking for anything’—do you have no liking for that view either?”
mn74:2.7: “Even if I liked this view of mine, Master Gotama, it would be the same, it would be the same.”[^2]
mn74:3.1: “Well, Aggivessana, there are more, indeed far more, in the world who say:
mn74:3.2: ‘it would be the same, it would be the same,’
mn74:3.3: and yet do not abandon that view and take up another view.
mn74:3.4: And there are fewer, indeed far fewer, in the world who say:
mn74:3.5: ‘it would be the same, it would be the same,’
mn74:3.6: and who abandon that view and do not take up another view.
mn74:4.1: There are, Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn74:4.3: there are, Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn74:4.5: and there are, Aggivessana, some ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn74:4.6: ‘I like some things, and I have no liking for some things.’
mn74:4.7: Of these, Aggivessana, the doctrine and view of those ascetics and brahmins who say: ‘I like everything’
mn74:4.8: is a view close to lust, close to bondage, close to relishing, close to holding, close to clinging;
mn74:4.9: and the doctrine and view of those ascetics and brahmins who say: ‘I have no liking for anything’
mn74:4.10: is a view close to non-lust, close to non-bondage, close to non-relishing, close to non-holding, close to non-clinging.”
mn74:5.1: When this was said, Dīghanakha the Wanderer said to the Blessed One:
mn74:5.2: “Master Gotama extols my view, Master Gotama commends my view.”
mn74:5.3: “Of these, Aggivessana, the ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn74:5.4: ‘I like some things, and I have no liking for some things’—
mn74:5.5: the part of their view that likes is close to lust, close to bondage, close to relishing, close to holding, close to clinging;
mn74:5.6: and the part of their view that has no liking is close to non-lust, close to non-bondage, close to non-relishing, close to non-holding, close to non-clinging.
mn74:6.1: “Of these, Aggivessana, the ascetics and brahmins whose doctrine and view is:
mn74:6.3: a wise man among them considers thus:
mn74:6.4: ‘If I were to adhere obstinately to this view of mine,
mn74:6.7: declaring: “Only this is true, everything else is wrong”—
mn74:6.8: then I would come into conflict with two others—
mn74:6.9: with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I have no liking for anything,”
mn74:6.10: and with the ascetic or brahmin whose doctrine and view is: “I like some things, and I have no liking for some things”—
mn74:6.11: I would come into conflict with these two.
mn74:6.12: Where there is conflict there is dispute; where there is dispute there is vexation; where there is vexation there is distress.’
mn74:6.13: So, seeing in himself this conflict, dispute, vexation, and distress, he abandons that view and does not take up another view.
mn74:6.14: That is how there comes to be the abandoning of these views, that is how there comes to be the relinquishing of these views.

mn74:9.1: Now, Aggivessana, this body possessed of form, made up of the four great elements, procreated by mother and father, built up out of rice and gruel, subject to impermanence, to being rubbed and massaged, to breaking apart and dispersal, should be regarded as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as void, as not self.
mn74:9.2: When one regards this body thus, as impermanent, as suffering, as a disease, as a boil, as a dart, as misery, as an affliction, as alien, as disintegrating, as void, as not self, one abandons desire for the body, affection for the body, and subservience to the body.[^3]
mn74:10.1: There are, Aggivessana, three kinds of feeling—
mn74:10.2: pleasant feeling, painful feeling, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling.
mn74:10.3: On the occasion, Aggivessana, when one feels pleasant feeling, one does not on that occasion feel painful feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
mn74:10.4: one feels only pleasant feeling on that occasion.
mn74:10.5: On the occasion when one feels painful feeling, one does not on that occasion feel pleasant feeling or neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
mn74:10.6: one feels only painful feeling on that occasion.
mn74:10.7: On the occasion when one feels neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling, one does not on that occasion feel pleasant feeling or painful feeling;
mn74:10.8: one feels only neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling on that occasion.
mn74:11.1: Pleasant feeling too, Aggivessana, is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, to falling away, to fading away, to cessation;
mn74:11.2: painful feeling too is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, to falling away, to fading away, to cessation;
mn74:11.3: and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling too is impermanent, conditioned, dependently arisen, subject to exhaustion, to falling away, to fading away, to cessation.
mn74:12.1: Seeing thus, Aggivessana, a well-taught noble disciple becomes disenchanted with pleasant feeling, becomes disenchanted with painful feeling, becomes disenchanted with neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling;
mn74:12.2: being disenchanted, his lust fades away; with the fading of lust he is liberated. When he is liberated, there comes the knowledge: “It is liberated.”
mn74:12.3: He understands: ‘Birth is exhausted, the life divine has been lived, what was to be done is done, there is no more of this to come.’
mn74:13.1: A bhikkhu whose mind is liberated thus, Aggivessana, does not side with anyone, does not dispute with anyone; he employs the current speech of the world without misapprehending it.”
mn74:14.1: Now on that occasion the venerable Sāriputta was standing behind the Blessed One, fanning him.
mn74:14.2: Then it occurred to the venerable Sāriputta:
mn74:14.3: “The Blessed One, it seems, speaks to us of the abandoning of these various things through direct knowledge; the Fortunate One, it seems, speaks to us of the relinquishing of these various things through direct knowledge.”
mn74:14.4: As the venerable Sāriputta considered this, his mind was liberated from the taints by non-clinging.
mn74:15.1: But in Dīghanakha the Wanderer there arose the spotless, immaculate vision of the Dhamma:
mn74:15.2: “Whatever is subject to arising is all subject to cessation.”
mn74:15.3: Then Dīghanakha the Wanderer, having seen the Dhamma, attained the Dhamma, understood the Dhamma, fathomed the Dhamma, having crossed beyond doubt, being free from perplexity, having gained intrepidity, and become independent of others in the Teacher’s dispensation, said to the Blessed One:
mn74:16.2: As though he were righting the overthrown, revealing the hidden, showing the way to one who was lost, holding up a lamp in the darkness so that those with eyes could see forms—so too the Dhamma has been made clear in many ways by Master Gotama.
mn74:16.3: I go to Master Gotama for refuge, and to the Dhamma, and to the Sangha of bhikkhus.
mn74:16.4: Let Master Gotama remember me as a lay follower who has gone to him for refuge from today for life.”
